title: Wise attention
hook: don't ask "did I exist in the past"; ask "what is dukkha, what ends it" (MN 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: asava, the taints, and seven ways to meet them. Your line: seven ways. Today, the first way: seeing.

Three in the morning, and the questions start. Who am I, really? What was I before all this? Will any of it matter? What if I've got everything wrong? You can turn those over for hours and get up more tired than you lay down. In an old discourse, the Buddha listed nearly the same questions, almost one for one. Then he said something surprising about them.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `WHO AM I? WHAT WAS I?` → `TIRED BY SUNRISE.`

segments.voice: In MN 2, the first way with the taints is seeing, and seeing depends on how you attend. Unwise attention comes first. A person wonders: Was I in the past? Was I not? What was I? Will I be in the future? What will I be? And now: Am I? Am I not? What am I? Where did this being come from, and where will it go? Then they settle on a view. I have a self. Or, I have no self. Or some other. The Buddha calls all of these a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a fetter of views. Notice that even I have no self is on that list, as a view to get tangled in. He doesn't call the people who ask foolish; he calls these questions unfit for attention. Then wise attention, yoniso manasikara. Manasikara is attention, literally making in the mind. Yoniso comes from yoni, a womb, a source: attention that goes back to where things come from. And it attends to this: this is dukkha; this is its arising; this is its ending; this is the way to its ending. The four noble truths, used as questions. A useful question changes something: where is the suffering in this, what's feeding it, what would ease it? And the text says attention like this cuts three fetters: the view of a fixed self, doubt, and clinging to rules and rituals. Not a small result, for changing what you ask.
screen: `WAS I? AM I? WHAT AM I?` · `A THICKET OF VIEWS.` · `YONISO — BACK TO THE SOURCE.` · `WHAT IS DUKKHA? WHAT ENDS IT?` · then, large: `THE USEFUL QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Find a question that's been circling lately, like why does this always happen to me, and hold it for a breath. Then turn it toward right now: where is the tension in the body, what's feeding it, what would ease it, even a little? No answers needed; just notice whether the new question sits differently.
Wise attention. Yoniso manasikara: attention that goes back to the source, and asks what is suffering and what ends it.
Your line: the useful question. It asks what would ease this, not who you really are. That's day four hundred four.

howItsDone: Teachers in many Buddhist schools emphasize wise attention, yoniso manasikara, as the ground of practice; Theravada teachers often present the four noble truths as a way of looking at any experience.

fork.reveal: MN 2 turns attention to the four truths: this is dukkha, its arising, its ending, the way. even 'I have no self' is listed as a view to get stuck in.

original.note: Pali yoniso manasikāra: wise attention, attention by way of the source.

trapdoor: what you thought: wise attention means paying close attention.
what it means: attention that goes back to the source and asks what suffering is and what ends it.
what a scholar hears: yoniso is an adverb from yoni, womb or origin; MN 2 lists six views, including both 'I have a self' and 'I have no self', as products of unwise attention.

chat.says: I lie awake asking who I really am. Isn't that the spiritual question?
options: The Buddha calls those a thicket; he points to what's suffering and what eases it.
Yes, the Buddha says losing sleep over it proves you're on track.
No, he says all questions are bad and the mind should simply go blank.
chat.meaning: In MN 2, questions like 'what am I?' lead into a thicket of views; wise attention asks about dukkha, its arising, ending and way.

yoniso.meaning: from yoni, a source: back to where things come from

manasikara.meaning: attention, literally making in the mind

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 2, Sabbasava Sutta (taints abandoned by seeing)
